item.title: I stopped clearing Windows caches after discovering it was silently costing me performance
item.itunes:title: I stopped clearing Windows caches after discovering it was silently costing me performance
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every once in a while, a Windows 11 optimization guide will tell you to "clear your cache" to reclaim some storage space on your SSD or speed up your PC. It's probably one of the most repeated maintenance tip that gets passed around on tech forums as well.

Most of the time, it's generally harmless, but depending on what you clear, you could be gaining just a few hundred megabytes of storage in exchange for long loading times and additionally making Windows and apps redo the work they have already done.

As with anything, there's a time and place for clearing caches, and that time is when your drive is running low on space or if something has gone wrong. Treating this method as routine maintenance can often be counterintuitive, though. Here's what the three most popular cleanup options remove, and what you sacrifice to get some space back.

The Settings cleanup is harmless, unless you tick two boxes

Thumbnail and shader cache aren't junk, whatever the list calls them

Perhaps the most popular way to clear cache on Windows 11 that most users will be familiar with is Settings > System > Storage > Temporary files. Through the Settings app, Windows gives you a list of things it considers "safe" to remove, but the problem with this familiar approach is that the list mixes leftovers with caches that your PC routinely requires.

Anything related to Delivery Optimization is fine to clear. These are the files that Windows downloads as a part of its update delivery system and stores temporarily so that updates can be shared with other PCs on your local network or the internet. Windows already manages this cache itself, sets a default cache expiration date (which is exactly 3 days) and the default maximum cache size is 20% of disk capacity.

The two that I prefer to leave alone are Thumbnails and DirectX Shader Cache. Windows Explorer uses its thumbnail cache to avoid rebuilding image and video previews every time you revisit a folder, while the Windows DirectX shader cache stores graphics work your games have already done. If you empty either, Windows and applications will simply start rebuilding it from scratch, and function slower than usual.

That being said, there are some special circumstances that warrant clearing the shader cache and thumbnail cache. For example, Epic Games recommends clearing the Nvidia DXCache (and the equivalent AMD DxCache on AMD systems) when titles like Fortnite deliver below the expected performance or if excessive stuttering is observed on DirectX12. It is worth noting that these are separate from the Windows DirectX Shader Cache entry.

You can also keep an eye on the size of the DXCache size through a utility called WizTree, which is how I discovered an Nvidia setting had allowed it to balloon up to 40GB, which is a rather disproportionate amount of storage for a cache whose job is to make games load and run more smoothly.

Similarly, a user might want to clear the thumbnail cache for a slightly different reason. Windows can retain thumbnail data even after the original files have been deleted, which can matter if you keep sensitive photos or use a shared PC. Outside these specific use cases though, there isn't much performance or storage to be reclaimed clearing these, and doing so only makes your PC work harder to rebuild them over time.

5 reasons you should avoid PC cleaning apps and use Windows Disk Cleanup instead

They're more trouble than they're worth

10
By  João Carrasqueira

Clearing Prefetch can make your app launches slower

It looks disposable, but Windows and your apps have a use for it

Windows introduced Prefetch in its Windows XP era, and it continues to persist on modern Windows 11 systems. What it does is basically record which files and resources an application requires during startup so that the OS can preload them more efficiently on every subsequent launch.

The common advice is to open C:\Windows\Prefetch and delete everything inside it to boost your system's performance. There's very little to gain from doing this, though. Not only is it redundant (Windows simply recreates the files as you launch those applications again), your frequently launched apps will be measurably slower upon startup, which hits your workflow where it hurts the most.

There are legitimate reasons to clear Prefetch, though, but as with the rest of the items I've listed, most of them involve troubleshooting specific Windows problems. As far as storage is concerned, there really isn't much to reclaim considering the size of the Prefetch folder on the average PC.

Manually emptying the Temp folder by hand skips a check Windows runs

It's not always wise to clear %temp%

One of the quickest ways to clear temporary files is to hit Windows + R, type in %temp%, and then select all and delete everything you find. On certain systems, it'll clear the most junk out of any other approach, but it also happens to be the bluntest in what it does.

Disk Cleanup (and Storage Sense) both deliberately skip temporary files that have been modified within the last seven days, and they do so because it's a built-in safety rule. Manually selecting and deleting everything in the %temp% folder, as you'd expect, ignores that filter entirely.

Microsoft's description of these temporary files says that programs usually clean up after themselves when they close, and anything that's left untouched for more than a week is generally safe to remove. Manual intervention here throws the seven-day rule out of the window. Deletion of some files may be blocked by an in-use error, but that's applied only to the files that are in use at the time when the action is performed.

The cost of this error is small, but nonetheless, noticeable. Microsoft's .NET documentation notes that single-file apps that use extraction unpack themselves into a .net folder inside the Temp directory before they run, so clearing it means they have to unpack all over again on the next launch.

8 ways you are unknowingly ruining your Windows experience

Windows habits that are secretly killing PC performance

4
By  Parth Shah

Not every cache file is junk

What most guides on the subject tend to forget (or omit) is the fact that caches exist because a process was slow the first time, and clearing it makes it slow all over again. That being said, there's merit in clearing cache files in certain specific situations, such as when an app is throwing errors, facing performance issues, or if a cache file is bloating beyond its usual size.

The key mistake that one should be mindful of is treating every cache file as junk. Likewise, deleting every cache file doesn't yield a measurable performance uplift or free up storage, and can often be counterproductive in practice.

item.title: 6 forgotten open-source apps that survived every productivity trend by keeping things simple
item.itunes:title: 6 forgotten open-source apps that survived every productivity trend by keeping things simple
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Productivity software has changed a lot over the years. Every few months, there seems to be a new app promising to organize my work, save time, or completely change how I get things done. I’ve tried plenty of those tools myself, and some have genuinely been useful. But I’ve also noticed that a few much older apps keep surviving every new wave. They may not have flashy interfaces or the latest features, but they continue to earn a spot on my PC. After using them for years, I’ve realized there is something valuable about software that simply stays useful without constantly trying to reinvent itself.

Everything

Fastest way to find files

Everything is one of those Windows apps I installed years ago and never really had a reason to remove. I often keep it open in the background because it makes finding files feel almost instant. Instead of digging through folders or remembering exactly where I saved something, I can start typing the filename and get to it quickly.

What I like most is how predictable it feels. I don't have to change how I work just because I'm using it. I type what I'm looking for, scan the results, and open the file. That's it.

I’ve used it for everything from tracking down old documents to finding files buried several folders deep. It has become one of those small utilities I barely think about until I have to use a computer without it. Then I immediately notice it's missing.

Everything
Individual pricing
Free
Platforms
Windows

Everything indexes all the files on your computer within seconds, and you can find any file or folder you are looking for quickly.

See at VoidTools

7-Zip

My go-to tool for archives

7-Zip is another old-school app that has quietly stayed on my computer for years. I use it whenever I need to package a group of files together or open an archive someone has sent me. It handles the job without making me think about which app should open the file or whether I need another tool installed.

I especially like how it fits naturally into File Explorer. I can right-click a file or folder, choose the 7-Zip option, and get the task done without opening a separate application first. It feels like a utility that belongs in Windows rather than something I have to actively manage.

There are plenty of newer archive tools around, but I rarely feel the need to look for alternatives. 7-Zip has been reliable enough that I simply keep using it whenever I need it.

7-Zip

7-Zip is the best and most powerful replacement for paid archiving software.

See at 7-Zip

Ditto

The old-school clipboard tool I trust

My clipboard used to be one of those small things that constantly interrupted my workflow. I would copy something, copy something else, and then realize I needed the previous item again. That changed once I started using Ditto.

I use it when writing, researching, and moving information between different apps. I can copy several pieces of text one after another and come back to them whenever I need. It is especially useful when I am collecting information from different sources and don't want to keep switching between windows.

What makes it stick around is how naturally it fits into my workflow. I don't need to plan around it or change how I work. I simply copy things as usual and use the clipboard history whenever I need something I copied earlier. It solves a small problem that comes up surprisingly often.

Ditto

Ditto is a simple clipboard manager for Windows that adds a lot more functionality, including the ability to remember copied files and retain items indefinitely.

See at Github See at Microsoft Store
5 open-source productivity tools that look and feel better than paid apps

Open-source apps that finally respect your attention.

8
By  Yash Patel

WinDirStat

My visual guide to disk space

Whenever my storage starts getting crowded, I like having a simple way to see what is actually taking up all that space. That is where WinDirStat still comes in handy for me. Instead of looking at a long list of folders and trying to guess which ones are responsible, I can scan a drive and get a visual breakdown of its contents.

The colorful blocks make it easy to spot unusually large files and folders without spending much time digging around. I find that especially useful when I know my storage is filling up but cannot immediately figure out why.

I don't use WinDirStat every day, but that is part of why I still keep it around. When I need to understand my disk usage, it gives me a clear picture quickly and lets me decide what actually needs my attention.

WinDirStat

WinDirStat is one of the best ways to visualize what's using your storage on a Windows PC.

See at Sourceforge

Notepad++

A no-fuss editor for everyday work

I still open Notepad++ whenever I need to quickly edit a text file without turning the task into a bigger project. It feels much lighter than opening a full development environment, especially when I only need to make a few changes. I use it for editing configuration files, checking snippets, or making quick changes to plain text.

The tabbed interface is another reason it has stayed in my workflow. I can keep several files open at once and switch between them without creating a mess of separate windows. Features like syntax highlighting and search also make it more useful than the basic Windows Notepad.

What I appreciate most is that it never tries to do too much. I can open it, make the changes I need, save the file, and close it. For small editing jobs, that simplicity still works for me.

Notepad++

Notepad++ is a free, open-source code editor for programmers and coders

See at Notepad++ See at PortableApps

VLC Media Player

The simple player that always works

There are still plenty of times when I just want to open a video or audio file and have it play without thinking about compatibility. That is when I turn to VLC Media Player. Over the years, I have come across all kinds of media files, and VLC has rarely given me a reason to search for another player.

I like that I can throw a file at it and usually get straight to watching or listening. I don't have to spend time figuring out which format I have or install a separate player for something unusual. The controls are also familiar enough that I never have to relearn the app.

I have tried newer media players over the years, but VLC keeps finding its way back onto my PC. It is one of those apps I install on every Windows setup without much thought.

VLC

VLC is one of the best open-source media players ever created.

See at VLC

By  Yash Patel

The apps I never feel the need to replace

After years of watching productivity software change, I’ve realized that I don’t always need the latest tool to improve my workflow. Some apps earn their place simply by being dependable and familiar. I may experiment with newer software, but I still come back to tools that have proven themselves over time. For me, that is what makes old-school software so difficult to replace.

item.title: Hints of the Steam Deck 2 begin to emerge as a leak reveals a mysterious "Gainsborough" APU
item.itunes:title: Hints of the Steam Deck 2 begin to emerge as a leak reveals a mysterious "Gainsborough" APU
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • AMD driver leak references 'Gainsborough' APU—strong hint a Steam Deck 2 is in the works.
  • Codename nod to 'Aerith'—Gainsborough is her surname, implying a direct sequel APU for the Deck.
  • Gainsborough likely N3P semi-custom chip for handhelds; Valve wants a generational leap—still unconfirmed.

With the Steam Machine, Steam Frame, and the new Steam Controller now available to purchase or preorder, there's a weird hole in Valve's hardware releases: where on earth is the Steam Deck 2? While the company hasn't confirmed or denied its existence, a recent leak points to a good possibility that one is currently in the works.

AMD's "Gainsborough" APU hints at a potential Steam Deck 2 release

Nothing has been confirmed, though

As reported on the YouTube channel Moore's Law is Dead, something interesting is happening with AMD APUs. Tucked away within the AMD drivers are references to something called "Gainsborough." While that's usually noteworthy in and of itself, mounting circumstantial evidence suggests "Gainsborough" will power the Steam Deck 2.

For instance, there's the codename. The original Steam Deck's APU used the codename "Aerith" from the classic RPG Final Fantasy VII. "Gainsborough" is her surname, so a new APU that uses the second half of her full name is pretty likely.

Next, Gainsborough seems to be equipped to handle TSMC's N3P node. This is one of the most efficient 3-nanometer variants available, and it would make complete sense if Gainsborough was destined to be used in handheld consoles—like the Steam Deck 2, for example.

Finally, it seems AMD designed Gainsborough as a semi-custom chip, rather than something that gets shipped to laptop and handheld manufacturers for general use. Moore's Law is Dead spoke with some of their insiders in the AMD OED scene, and none of them had heard of Gainsborough, which strongly hints that the APU will find itself in a specific product.

Valve isn't ditching Windows or x86, but it's quietly making both optional

Valve wants to make it possible for gamers to play anywhere.

3
By  Adam Conway

The timeline lines up with a Steam Deck 2 release

Things are looking likely for a new console

Alright, so how likely is it that this is evidence that the Steam Deck 2 is in production? Well, from what we can tell from outside of Valve's HQ, the chances of it working on a new Steam Deck are pretty high. Lawrence Yang of Valve confirmed two years ago that Valve was interested in making a Steam Deck 2, but it didn't want to simply release a console with marginally higher specs, as it would be unfair to its consumers:

​​​​​​​"So, we really do want to wait for a generational leap in compute without sacrificing battery life before we ship the real second generation of Steam Deck. But it is something that we're excited about and we're working on."

Moore's Law is Dead speculated that a Steam Deck 2 based on this hardware would be akin to upgrading an Xbox One to an Xbox Series X or a PlayStation 5, which would likely be a strong enough reason to convince Valve to release a new handheld console. Alas, as is the norm with these leaks, nothing has been outright stated and should be taken with a grain of salt until confirmed otherwise.

Someone squeezed the Steam Deck's hardware into a custom Game Boy shell, and it looks amazing

Hey Valve, maybe take some notes from this one.

item.title: I changed my Fire TV Stick’s DNS to unlock more content, but it fixed something even more annoying
item.itunes:title: I changed my Fire TV Stick’s DNS to unlock more content, but it fixed something even more annoying
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
In the past, I have often managed to bypass geo-blocking and other restrictions by switching DNS servers. It's the most feasible option, since a VPN generally slows down your connection. So, I tried the same with my Fire TV Stick, and to my surprise, it fixed a much bigger problem, something that I wasn't even actively focused on.

For those who are unaware, DNS or Domain Name System, often called the internet's phone book, is simply put, a database. While we use domain names like "xda-developers.com" to access websites, machines use IP addresses. And this is where DNS comes into the picture. It translates human-readable domain names into machine-readable IP addresses. The problem is that the default DNS on routers and devices isn't always the best for performance, and switching to another DNS server can do wonders.

It improved connectivity

Faster loading and less buffering

As surprising as it may sound, changing your Fire TV Stick's DNS, or even the one on your smart TV, improves connectivity and minimizes related issues. Also, content loads faster and buffers less, as long as you're on a decent internet plan. If the internet speed itself is slow, switching DNS won't do much good.

Let's understand how switching DNS can help with streaming. A better-performing DNS connects your Fire TV Stick to a better server, improving load times. This difference in performance becomes noticeable if the default DNS is slow, overloaded, or directing you to a less-than-optimal server. For my Fire TV Stick, I picked Cloudflare's DNS since it's one of the most reliable, at least as far as I know. Google's public DNS is good too, and I would have tried it next had Cloudflare's DNS not performed well. But it didn't come down to that. Maybe I will try Google's in a week or so.

Keep in mind that you can also change the router's DNS. Since I was simply trying to bypass content restrictions on the Fire TV Stick, I didn't want to reconfigure things at the network level. But that should work too, if you are more comfortable with that.

6 useful Fire TV Stick apps that really improve my streaming experience

Stop scrolling, start streaming.

3
By  Parth Shah

Changing DNS on Fire TV Stick is simple

It takes about two minutes

You can easily change the DNS on your Fire TV Stick. It's not as straightforward as switching DNS on a PC, but it's pretty simple. First, open Settings on your Fire TV Stick, go to Device and Software, then into About, and scroll down to Network. You should now see the IP address, Gateway, and current DNS on the right. Take a picture of this, as we'll need this information in a minute.

Now, go back to Settings, then into Network, select the connected network, and choose Forget this network. Then reselect the network from the list, enter the password, and select "Advanced" at the bottom. It will now ask you for the IP address. Enter what you captured in the picture earlier. Similarly, fill out the Gateway field. For Network Prefix Length, enter the number currently shown in the field, then proceed. You will now be asked for the DNS details. Since we are using Cloudflare's DNS, enter 1.1.1.1 under DNS 1 and 1.0.0.1 under DNS 2. That's it. Your Fire TV Stick now has a new DNS.

To confirm everything is in order, do a quick reboot, then check whether the new DNS holds. For most of you, it should. But it is still worth checking.

It won't unlock more content

You are better off with a dedicated service

Frankly, switching to Cloudflare's DNS didn't do what I expected, and I was a little disappointed at first. But as soon as I realized that it improves the streaming experience, it felt like I should have made the switch long ago. For a streaming stick or even a smart TV, the streaming experience is far more important than bypassing restrictions and unlocking more content.

That said, you can unlock more content by changing your DNS settings. You absolutely can, but you will need a specialized smart DNS service. Options range from Smart DNS Proxy to SniDust. They aren't as secure as a VPN because a smart DNS service doesn't encrypt your traffic, but it also doesn't slow down your connection, which can be a real damper.

Setting up a local DNS was one of the easiest improvements I made to my home network

Having local control opens up so many possibilities

14
By  Joe Rice-Jones

A simple change can upgrade your streaming experience

So, if you are looking to upgrade the streaming experience on your Fire TV Stick, switching DNS is one of the easier options. Other built-in features are worth exploring, too. Keep in mind this may not work for everyone, and switching to a more crowded DNS may make things worse.

But as long as you are a little smart about the changes, it's worth a try, given that there are no major downsides to switching to Cloudflare's or Google's DNS.

item.title: I turned my desktop into a remote coding server using VS Code's hidden tunnel feature
item.itunes:title: I turned my desktop into a remote coding server using VS Code's hidden tunnel feature
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve stuck with VS Code because of its maturity and the features I keep discovering. Its extension ecosystem is hard to match, but there’s more to it than extensions. It has built-in voice-to-text that runs locally on your computer, and Remote SSH lets you use the hardware of a coding server even when you’re working from a budget laptop.

More recently, I found Tunnels tucked away in the Accounts menu. It works a lot like Remote SSH, but you can use your desktop as a coding server, then access it from another device through a browser without installing VS Code there. I’ve set it up on my desktop and have been using it frequently.

VS Code Tunnels is a godsend feature

It’s useful in so many ways

Remote Tunnels lets you use one computer’s coding environment from another device. VS Code runs a server on the computer you want to access and connects it to a browser or another VS Code installation through a secure tunnel. Your files stay on that computer, and it handles terminal commands, debugging, and extensions that run against the project. You’re working on the remote machine without streaming its entire desktop.

The browser access makes this especially useful. You can use VS Code web for light editing but it cannot run a project on your desktop. However, once you connect it through a tunnel, you can use your desktop’s development environment from a budget laptop or even a tablet. You also don’t need to make the desktop reachable from the internet, open ports, or set up an SSH server.

This is especially helpful when you’re traveling. Developer friends have told me VS Code Tunnels lets them travel with a lighter, less powerful machine and connect to their home computer without dealing with firewall configuration. I’ve even traveled with just an iPad, without having to move my files off my PC. You can leave your code and hardware on your desktop and still access them through a browser, which is a godsend.

Better than billion-dollar software.

By  Parth Shah

I can get to my desktop from a browser

That alone makes this worthwhile

The option is easy to miss. On the desktop you want to access remotely, open VS Code’s Accounts menu and select Turn on Remote Tunnel Access. After you sign in, VS Code gives you a vscode.dev link for that machine. You can also start a tunnel with code tunnel from the command line, but the Accounts menu is the simpler route when VS Code is already open.

The main caveat is that your computer has to stay on, and VS Code has to keep running for the tunnel to remain available. That’s manageable with a desktop PC, whether it’s a Mac mini or a custom build. It’s less convenient with a laptop, which you’d need to leave running and plugged in for long periods. If your coding setup is already on a desktop, you can leave the tunnel available and connect whenever you need it.

Once you have enabled the feature, open the tunnel link on another device, sign in with the account used to set up access, and you get a VS Code window in the browser connected to your desktop. You can open folders, edit files, and use a terminal running on the remote machine. Commands and supported extensions run there too.

Tunnels is easier to live with than Remote SSH

Tunnels requires much less setup

I’ve used Remote SSH plenty, and it works well for servers I already have access to. Setting up a new machine takes more work. It needs an SSH server, login credentials, and a way for my laptop to reach it. If that machine is at home and I’m elsewhere, I also need to sort out access to my home network.

With my desktop, I turned on Tunnels from VS Code’s Accounts menu and signed in. Now I can connect to it through the same account, whether I’m using VS Code on another computer or opening vscode.dev in a browser. I don’t have to set up SSH on the desktop or configure each device I might use to reach it.

Of course, comparing the two isn’t exactly apples to apples. Remote SSH is geared more toward enterprise environments, where anyone with the necessary credentials can connect to a server from virtually anywhere. For accessing my desktop, however, Tunnels is more convenient because I can enable it directly in VS Code and return to my coding setup from another device.

VS Code is still my daily driver

There have been times when I’ve ditched VS Code and used another IDE for a while. For example, I recently switched to Cursor and also tried Zed, while giving IDEs like Antigravity and others a shot. But I keep coming back to VS Code because there simply isn’t another IDE I find as reliable. I’ll admit that it isn’t the fastest, and I don’t appreciate the telemetry Microsoft has added, but all in all, it’s still the platform I would use as my daily driver.

item.title: Synology's health check missed 9,527 errors on my drive, and I only found them by asking directly
item.itunes:title: Synology's health check missed 9,527 errors on my drive, and I only found them by asking directly
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My first NAS was an unfamiliar device for me. I won it on a random giveaway, and for the first couple of years, it sat in my storage room, as I was in my sophomore year living in a hostel. After I graduated and moved back to my home, I started using it.

For years, it was simply used for bulk storage, since it was a weak two-bay DS218j NAS. But last week, an online article led to checking my drive’s SMART data. Synology’s DSM only showed me a healthy status, but I wanted to see what led to that verdict.

What the Synology dashboard shows you

Every screen says healthy, and none of them say why

I am no expert in drives and storage tech, but since I own a few storage devices myself, I follow the news. Last week I was reading about a hard drive study, and that led me to check my hard drive data as well. My old Synology NAS has only one Toshiba HDD installed.

I think if you are already into NAS and storage devices, you are already familiar with SMART. In case you aren't, every modern drive comes with a built-in monitoring system, known as Self-Monitoring, Analysis, and Reporting Technology, or SMART.

As usual, I opened DSM to check the stats, hoping Synology would give me all the information I needed. Specifically, I was looking for Backblaze’s five SMART attributes — 5, 187, 188, 197, and 198.

  • 5 is Reallocated_Sector_Ct,
  • 187 is Reported_Uncorrectable_Errors,
  • 188 is Command_Timeout,
  • 197 is Current_Pending_Sector,
  • 198 is Offline_Uncorrectable.

Collectively, they cover sectors being remapped, unreadable data, command problems, and pending/uncorrectable sectors, and Backblaze uses them to flag failing drives. In Storage Manager, the overview page only showed a green tick with a healthy label. Nothing else. Then I moved to the HDD/SSD section and checked my HDD’s health info. Again, the health info window gave me nothing important, just the basic info.

The overview tab showed me a 36°C temperature and a 29,336 power-on hours record. The S.M.A.R.T. tab offered Quick and Extended tests, and the last test result showed a healthy status. And finally, the History tab, which had absolutely nothing. I even tried to run a quick test, but the results did change.

I was expecting the five Backblaze attributes, but Synology exposed none of them and gave me just a simple label saying my drive is alright. But I wasn’t going to stop there and take Synology’s word as is. So, I stopped looking in the DSM GUI and went looking for the SMART data underneath it.

I stopped relying entirely on my NAS temperature warnings

After Google studied 100,000 drives.

By  Shivansh Raj Srivastava

What the drive reports when you ask directly

Three clean numbers, and two that don't exist

Since the DSM diagnostics proved useless, the next obvious thing was to directly ask the drive to give me those numbers. I enabled the NAS’s SSH access over port 22, connected to it via Termius, and ran smartctl -d sat -A /dev/sdb.

Starting with the good news, it turned out my Toshiba drive was only reporting 5, 197, and 198 out of the five Backblaze attributes, and they were all clean. The reported raw values for all three were 0. Presumably, that was why the DSM showed healthy in the dashboard.

But there is a catch. The reported THRESH for SMART 5 was 5, and the reported RAW_VALUE was 0, so it is clean with no remapped sectors. For SMART 197 and 198, the reported THRESH was 0. That means 197 and 198 effectively never trip the drive's own failure flag. Anyway, they’re both labeled as aging indicators (Old_age) by the vendor, so I didn’t dig deep.

The two attributes the drive didn’t report were 187 and 188. This wasn’t something that DSM was hiding. What I could figure out is this particular Toshiba drive doesn't include them in its SMART table. They were both kind of important metrics, but since they weren’t present at all, I'm leaving them out.

I started to look for five Backblaze attributes. I found three of them, and none gave me a dramatic finding. But while looking at the full SMART table, I found another attribute, and it was the odd one.

The one number that scared me

9,527 errors, and none in 25,000 hours

While looking at the full SMART table, another completely different attribute stood out, SMART 199. The table reported it as UDMA_CRC_Error_Count. It wasn’t one of Backblaze’s five but looked genuinely alarming. The reported raw value was 9,527.

After some quick research, what I understood is that this is the count when the drive ran a command and came back with an error. So, 9,527 was the error count, and the log only kept the last five of them with their corresponding power-on hours. Those five errors appear to be Interface CRC (ICRC) errors, typically checksum failures on the cable. And the highest numbered (#9527) error was the newest, and it occurred at 4,312 power-on hours.

I remembered seeinf my drive’s power-on hours on DSM as well; I quickly navigated to the Storage Manager to match those. The recorded power-on hours were 29,339. That means the last reported error was roughly 25,000 power-on hours earlier, and it hasn’t increased since then. At that moment, the scary number became less alarming because the count became history instead of a live fault.

I expected DSM to give me detailed statistics of my hard drive, but it only gave me one word: “Healthy.” It didn’t show either the five Backblaze attributes or the 199 counter I got from the SMART table directly from the drive. If DSM tracked those errors over time, I could have reconstructed when those remaining 9,522 errors occurred.

Why my NAS backups failed, and what I wish I’d noticed sooner 

How small oversights nearly erased months of data

By  Karandeep Singh

The drive passed, and I'm still not sure

This was just a single drive, one 6-year-old NAS, and one snapshot of its SMART data. Even though the reported Backblaze SMART attributes look fine and DSM showed a healthy label, that doesn’t mean the drive is in good condition and would never fail. I know my drive. I know it is old enough to be retired. But the attributes say otherwise. So, the SMART data is useful, but it shouldn't be the only data to be considered the final deciding factor.

  • 5 is Reallocated_Sector_Ct,
  • 187 is Reported_Uncorrectable_Errors,
  • 188 is Command_Timeout,
  • 197 is Current_Pending_Sector,
  • 198 is Offline_Uncorrectable.

Collectively, they cover sectors being remapped, unreadable data, command problems, and pending/uncorrectable sectors, and Backblaze uses them to flag failing drives. In Storage Manager, the overview page only showed a green tick with a healthy label. Nothing else. Then I moved to the HDD/SSD section and checked my HDD’s health info. Again, the health info window gave me nothing important, just the basic info.

The overview tab showed me a 36°C temperature and a 29,336 power-on hours record. The S.M.A.R.T. tab offered Quick and Extended tests, and the last test result showed a healthy status. And finally, the History tab, which had absolutely nothing. I even tried to run a quick test, but the results did change.

I was expecting the five Backblaze attributes, but Synology exposed none of them and gave me just a simple label saying my drive is alright. But I wasn’t going to stop there and take Synology’s word as is. So, I stopped looking in the DSM GUI and went looking for the SMART data underneath it.

I stopped relying entirely on my NAS temperature warnings

After Google studied 100,000 drives.

By  Shivansh Raj Srivastava

What the drive reports when you ask directly

Three clean numbers, and two that don't exist

Since the DSM diagnostics proved useless, the next obvious thing was to directly ask the drive to give me those numbers. I enabled the NAS’s SSH access over port 22, connected to it via Termius, and ran smartctl -d sat -A /dev/sdb.

Starting with the good news, it turned out my Toshiba drive was only reporting 5, 197, and 198 out of the five Backblaze attributes, and they were all clean. The reported raw values for all three were 0. Presumably, that was why the DSM showed healthy in the dashboard.

But there is a catch. The reported THRESH for SMART 5 was 5, and the reported RAW_VALUE was 0, so it is clean with no remapped sectors. For SMART 197 and 198, the reported THRESH was 0. That means 197 and 198 effectively never trip the drive's own failure flag. Anyway, they’re both labeled as aging indicators (Old_age) by the vendor, so I didn’t dig deep.

The two attributes the drive didn’t report were 187 and 188. This wasn’t something that DSM was hiding. What I could figure out is this particular Toshiba drive doesn't include them in its SMART table. They were both kind of important metrics, but since they weren’t present at all, I'm leaving them out.

I started to look for five Backblaze attributes. I found three of them, and none gave me a dramatic finding. But while looking at the full SMART table, I found another attribute, and it was the odd one.

The one number that scared me

9,527 errors, and none in 25,000 hours

While looking at the full SMART table, another completely different attribute stood out, SMART 199. The table reported it as UDMA_CRC_Error_Count. It wasn’t one of Backblaze’s five but looked genuinely alarming. The reported raw value was 9,527.

After some quick research, what I understood is that this is the count when the drive ran a command and came back with an error. So, 9,527 was the error count, and the log only kept the last five of them with their corresponding power-on hours. Those five errors appear to be Interface CRC (ICRC) errors, typically checksum failures on the cable. And the highest numbered (#9527) error was the newest, and it occurred at 4,312 power-on hours.

I remembered seeinf my drive’s power-on hours on DSM as well; I quickly navigated to the Storage Manager to match those. The recorded power-on hours were 29,339. That means the last reported error was roughly 25,000 power-on hours earlier, and it hasn’t increased since then. At that moment, the scary number became less alarming because the count became history instead of a live fault.

I expected DSM to give me detailed statistics of my hard drive, but it only gave me one word: “Healthy.” It didn’t show either the five Backblaze attributes or the 199 counter I got from the SMART table directly from the drive. If DSM tracked those errors over time, I could have reconstructed when those remaining 9,522 errors occurred.

Why my NAS backups failed, and what I wish I’d noticed sooner 

How small oversights nearly erased months of data

By  Karandeep Singh

The drive passed, and I'm still not sure

This was just a single drive, one 6-year-old NAS, and one snapshot of its SMART data. Even though the reported Backblaze SMART attributes look fine and DSM showed a healthy label, that doesn’t mean the drive is in good condition and would never fail. I know my drive. I know it is old enough to be retired. But the attributes say otherwise. So, the SMART data is useful, but it shouldn't be the only data to be considered the final deciding factor.

item.title: My 6-year old GPU still handles modern games better than what the marketing wants you to believe
item.itunes:title: My 6-year old GPU still handles modern games better than what the marketing wants you to believe
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
GPU companies always want to sell you the latest thing, just like any business would. Today, it's Nvidia's RTX 50 and AMD's RX 90 series graphics cards. Packing greater performance and more advanced ray tracing and upscaling features than whatever came before, these GPUs are supposedly necessary for running the latest games the way they're "meant to be played."

However, my 6-year-old RTX 3080 is still going strong in the latest titles, despite being around 40% slower than the RTX 5080 and missing cutting-edge DLSS features found on the latest Nvidia cards. It turns out that you don't need the latest and greatest GPU to enjoy PC gaming even if you're playing demanding AAA games.

I tested these "old" GPUs with 2026 AAA games, and the results were weirdly encouraging

Your old GPU might be more future-proof than you think

6
By  Samarveer Singh

You don't need DLSS Frame Gen to enjoy modern games

Despite what Nvidia says

  • Credit: Nvidia.com
  • Credit: Nvidia.com

Ever since Nvidia failed to deliver impressive generational gains with their RTX 50 series cards, they've been leaning heavily into their frame generation capabilities. While it's true that most gamers won't notice the latency penalty that comes with the technology, you can still get playable framerates without it. My RTX 3080 doesn't support DLSS Frame Generation, not even the 2x variant found on the RTX 40 series cards, but it's still a capable GPU.

The RTX 30 series has access to all the latest DLSS 4.5 features except frame generation. This gives me access to the latest transformer model that powers advanced upscaling in supported titles. Plus, I can also enable Ray Reconstruction and DLAA for better denoising and anti-aliasing. So, the RTX 30 series isn't exactly "outdated" in 2026.

The RTX 3080 launched in 2020, and it was somewhat of an anomaly from the Nvidia camp. Its price-to-performance hasn't been replicated by Nvidia ever since. In fact, the company has worked hard not to repeat the RTX 3080 "mistake." The RTX 4080 and RTX 5080 are significantly faster than my Ampere card, but the value proposition just isn't there.

GDDR7 pricing is holding the 50-Super series hostage, and it just cost me my next upgrade

GPU upgrade dreams continue to be shattered by the relentless AI demand

1
By  Abhinav Raj

Getting 60+ FPS on my 1440p ultrawide monitor is no joke

I can keep the current setup going for a few more years

I upgraded from a 1440p IPS monitor to a 3440x1440 ultrawide OLED display a year ago, and my average framerates naturally took a big hit. Despite that, my RTX 3080 stood its ground in most of the latest titles, delivering a smooth 60–80 FPS at a mix of High and Ultra settings. I've also dialed in a slight undervolt to keep the temperatures in check, since the RTX 3080 can frequently hit throttling temperatures without it.

I benchmarked the card in several modern titles, such as Still Wakes the Deep, Forza Horizon 6, and Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy. Without ray tracing enabled, each of the three games ran comfortably above 70 FPS, with Forza Horizon 6 churning out 90+ FPS.

3440x1440 - High/Ultra settings

Average FPS

Still Wakes the Deep

76

Forza Horizon 6

91

Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy

75

In other games like Cyberpunk 2077, Alan Wake 2, and Black Myth: Wukong, where ray tracing is a substantial visual upgrade, DLSS Balanced/Performance keeps my framerate more than playable. Besides, FSR frame generation is always an option when my FPS threatens to dip below 60 FPS.

I tested the RTX 3080 against the RTX 5080, and upgrading isn't worth it yet

In Forza Horizon 6 and other AAA titles, the RTX 3080 is still viable

27
By  Ty Sherback

RTX 30 owners don't need to upgrade yet

Not like you can upgrade in this market anyway

Credit: Source: Nvidia
 

Nvidia may be pushing its RTX 50 series cards on you with its aggressive marketing, but many RTX 30 series owners don't necessarily need to switch. As long as you have an upper-mid-range or high-end model like the RTX 3070 Ti, RTX 3080, or RTX 3090, you can safely skip an upgrade for now. Unless you're gaming at 4K resolution, your GPU can still deliver the goods at 1440p High settings in most new titles.

The current market isn't conducive to a GPU upgrade anyway. In fact, the RAM shortage has inflated the prices of nearly every PC component these days, and things don't seem to be getting better anytime soon. The RTX 5080 has crossed $1,600 at the time of writing, so I'm more than happy to get some more mileage out of my RTX 3080. All I'm praying for is that my GPU doesn't die on me out of the blue.

The RTX 3080 was supposed to be old by now, but the RTX 60 delay handed it two more years

I don't need to upgrade my RTX 3080 for a few more years

3
By  Tanveer Singh

My two-generation old GPU is enough for modern gaming

I'm glad that my RTX 3080 still packs a punch in the latest AAA titles. I can even enable ray tracing in some games as long as DLSS upscaling helps keep things smooth. Despite not supporting DLSS frame generation, I can use FSR frame generation or OptiScaler to boost my framerates further, not that I need to just yet. GPU pricing will probably get worse before it gets better, so it's better to delay your upgrades.

item.title: I replaced Notion, Figma, and my task app with one Obsidian setup, and I haven't looked back
item.itunes:title: I replaced Notion, Figma, and my task app with one Obsidian setup, and I haven't looked back
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I used to think I needed a separate app for every part of my workflow. I had apps like Obsidian, Notion, Figma, and TickTick in my setup. It worked, but constantly jumping between apps started to feel like unnecessary friction.

So I decided to see how far I could push Obsidian instead. With the right views, plugins, and a bit of customization, I turned a simple Markdown-based note-taking app into a workspace that now handles my everyday workflow.

4 game-changing Obsidian workflows I wish I tried earlier

Obsidian workflows I tried late, but you don’t have to

4
By  Parth Shah

My productivity stack had become fragmented

I was maintaining the same work everywhere

My productivity setup worked, but it was spread across too many apps. I used Obsidian for notes and research, Notion for databases and project tracking, Figma for diagrams and visual planning and a separate task app for deadlines. The problem was the constant context switching.

I would outline an article in one app, track its status somewhere else, keep related tasks in another place, and then open Figma whenever I needed to map out an idea. None of these tools was the problem individually, but together they made my workflow feel unnecessarily fragmented. I wanted one place where everything could actually connect.

Bases replaced my Notion databases

My notes became the database

Notion databases were one of the hardest things for me to give up because they are quite flexible. Obsidian Bases isn’t quite on that level yet, but for the way I manage my work, it gets very close.

I can use properties to track things like article status, publication, deadline, category, priority, and publish date, and then surface that information in table, list, or card layouts depending on what I need. A table works well for my article pipeline, while cards are better when I want a more visual overview of projects or ideas.

What really changed things for me is that Bases is built directly into Obsidian. I don’t need to install and maintain a third-party database plugin just to create structured views of my notes.

The underlying files are still regular Markdown notes, but Bases gives me a cleaner way to organize and filter them. Again, it isn’t as powerful as Notion, but for my workflow, it is more than enough.

Mermaid handles diagrams without another app

Throw in Canvas and Excalidraw in the mix

Mermaid takes care of most of the structured diagrams I used to create elsewhere. Since it works directly inside Markdown, I can quickly build flowcharts, process maps, and simple architecture diagrams without leaving Obsidian.

When I need something more free-form, I switch to Canvas or the Excalidraw plugin. Canvas is great for brainstorming because I can spread ideas across an infinite board, connect them visually, and drop actual Obsidian notes right into the workspace.

Excalidraw goes a step further when I want to sketch something quickly, such as a website layout, user flow, or rough mockup for a client. The part I like most is how everything stays connected.

I can create a quick website mockup in Excalidraw and keep the related requirements, client notes, copy ideas, and project documentation right beside it.

4 lightweight open-source tools that replaced all of my paid apps

Free, fast, and fully capable

1
By  Nolen Jonker

I stopped needing a separate task app

Tasks now live with my work

Task management was another area where I expected Obsidian to fall short, but Daily Notes ended up covering most of what I needed. I use my daily page as a simple command center for the day, with deadlines, writing priorities, follow-ups, and quick tasks all in one place.

Since those tasks sit alongside my notes, I don’t have to jump into a separate app just to remember why something needs to be done.

For more advanced task management, I use the third-party Tasks plugin. It lets me add due dates, priorities, recurring tasks, and queries that pull unfinished items from across my vault into a single view. That means I can keep a task inside the article or project note where it belongs, while still seeing everything due today or this week from one dashboard.

For my workflow, that was enough to replace a dedicated task manager. I also customized the way I navigate Obsidian. A plugin like Beautitab gives me a cleaner, search-engine-like start page, so opening Obsidian feels like launching a workspace.

I have added a motivational quote, inserted a background picture, and customized the entire experience so that I can quickly search for a note, project, or idea and get straight back to work.

My entire workflow lives in Obsidian

I don’t think Obsidian is suddenly a better version of Notion, Figma, and every dedicated task manager. Those apps still go much deeper in their respective areas. But I also realized I wasn’t using most of that depth. Now, everything revolves around the same local Markdown files, so my notes, projects, tasks, and ideas finally feel like parts of one system.

Of course, this is just my setup. Obsidian is highly customizable. So what are you waiting for? Get creative with your vault and get the best out of this gem.

I used to think I needed a separate app for every part of my workflow. I had apps like Obsidian, Notion, Figma, and TickTick in my setup. It worked, but constantly jumping between apps started to feel like unnecessary friction.

So I decided to see how far I could push Obsidian instead. With the right views, plugins, and a bit of customization, I turned a simple Markdown-based note-taking app into a workspace that now handles my everyday workflow.

4 game-changing Obsidian workflows I wish I tried earlier

Obsidian workflows I tried late, but you don’t have to

4
By  Parth Shah

My productivity stack had become fragmented

I was maintaining the same work everywhere

My productivity setup worked, but it was spread across too many apps. I used Obsidian for notes and research, Notion for databases and project tracking, Figma for diagrams and visual planning and a separate task app for deadlines. The problem was the constant context switching.

I would outline an article in one app, track its status somewhere else, keep related tasks in another place, and then open Figma whenever I needed to map out an idea. None of these tools was the problem individually, but together they made my workflow feel unnecessarily fragmented. I wanted one place where everything could actually connect.

Bases replaced my Notion databases

My notes became the database

Notion databases were one of the hardest things for me to give up because they are quite flexible. Obsidian Bases isn’t quite on that level yet, but for the way I manage my work, it gets very close.

I can use properties to track things like article status, publication, deadline, category, priority, and publish date, and then surface that information in table, list, or card layouts depending on what I need. A table works well for my article pipeline, while cards are better when I want a more visual overview of projects or ideas.

What really changed things for me is that Bases is built directly into Obsidian. I don’t need to install and maintain a third-party database plugin just to create structured views of my notes.

The underlying files are still regular Markdown notes, but Bases gives me a cleaner way to organize and filter them. Again, it isn’t as powerful as Notion, but for my workflow, it is more than enough.

Mermaid handles diagrams without another app

Throw in Canvas and Excalidraw in the mix

Mermaid takes care of most of the structured diagrams I used to create elsewhere. Since it works directly inside Markdown, I can quickly build flowcharts, process maps, and simple architecture diagrams without leaving Obsidian.

When I need something more free-form, I switch to Canvas or the Excalidraw plugin. Canvas is great for brainstorming because I can spread ideas across an infinite board, connect them visually, and drop actual Obsidian notes right into the workspace.

Excalidraw goes a step further when I want to sketch something quickly, such as a website layout, user flow, or rough mockup for a client. The part I like most is how everything stays connected.

I can create a quick website mockup in Excalidraw and keep the related requirements, client notes, copy ideas, and project documentation right beside it.

4 lightweight open-source tools that replaced all of my paid apps

Free, fast, and fully capable

1
By  Nolen Jonker

I stopped needing a separate task app

Tasks now live with my work

Task management was another area where I expected Obsidian to fall short, but Daily Notes ended up covering most of what I needed. I use my daily page as a simple command center for the day, with deadlines, writing priorities, follow-ups, and quick tasks all in one place.

Since those tasks sit alongside my notes, I don’t have to jump into a separate app just to remember why something needs to be done.

For more advanced task management, I use the third-party Tasks plugin. It lets me add due dates, priorities, recurring tasks, and queries that pull unfinished items from across my vault into a single view. That means I can keep a task inside the article or project note where it belongs, while still seeing everything due today or this week from one dashboard.

For my workflow, that was enough to replace a dedicated task manager. I also customized the way I navigate Obsidian. A plugin like Beautitab gives me a cleaner, search-engine-like start page, so opening Obsidian feels like launching a workspace.

I have added a motivational quote, inserted a background picture, and customized the entire experience so that I can quickly search for a note, project, or idea and get straight back to work.

My entire workflow lives in Obsidian

I don’t think Obsidian is suddenly a better version of Notion, Figma, and every dedicated task manager. Those apps still go much deeper in their respective areas. But I also realized I wasn’t using most of that depth. Now, everything revolves around the same local Markdown files, so my notes, projects, tasks, and ideas finally feel like parts of one system.

Of course, this is just my setup. Obsidian is highly customizable. So what are you waiting for? Get creative with your vault and get the best out of this gem.

item.itunes:title: Thanks to fans, the original Halo just got an unofficial Windows, Linux, PS5, and Android port
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • This community built port brings Halo: Combat Evolved to Windows, Linux, Android, PS4/PS5 (jailbreak needed) and more.
  • It features the full campaign and 128-player multiplayer.
  • You need to supply a Xbox Halo disc image (.iso/.xiso) to play.

I recently covered the browser-based port of Halo: Combat Evolved, and now I'm back with more great Halo news. A community-powered effort has unofficially ported the original Halo: Combat Evolved to several platforms, including Windows, Linux, Android, and PS5.

The ports feature the full campaign and multiplayer, including support for up to 128 players, which, if you're as familiar with the Halo series as I am, is absolutely wild. Imagine a 128-player Death Match in Blood Gulch? Of course, on PlayStation 5, you'll need a jailbroken console to run the iconic first-person shooter.

All of these ports follow a recently released decompilation of Halo: Combat Evolved by bnunu called Halo-1, which is a based on punpckhdq's Halo decompilation efforts. Of course, like most modern retro game ports, this project was almost certainly developed with significant AI help, though the decompilation's GitHub page doesn't disclose that.

Like all retro game decompilations, you'll need an Xbox disc image of Halo: Combat Evolved to play the port. The port is compatible with .xiso and .iso Halo: Combat Evolved disc images from all versions of the title. Of course, this means you'll need to dump the disc you already own, though you can also find OG Halo disc images elsewhere on the internet if you know where to look.

If you want to try the port yourself, you can find cybersecurity's halo-ce-universal GitHub page at this link.

Given the Halo series’ struggles over the years, it’s refreshing to see fans breathe new life into the game that started it all

It will be very interesting to see what mods are created for the port

Credit: cybersecurity / GitHub

The Halo series has run into significant issues over the past few years, including Halo Infinite failing to live up to Microsoft's lofty live-service expectations and the recently released Halo: Campaign Evolved remake launching to a mixed reception.

I recently played through Campaign Evolved and really enjoyed the remaster, though it definitely has several issues, including stability problems, less-than-stellar cinematics, and an overall atmosphere shift that doesn't feel like it always vibes quite right. Still, I had fun with the remaster, especially the latter half of the game that features the Flood.

More recently, Microsoft basically shut down Halo Studios (formerly 343 Industries) and handed over the series' development to Activision. With all the negativity surrounding the long-running series lately, it's great to see dedicated Halo fans release a project like this, even if it was likely created with AI help. I'm very excited to see what mods end up getting created for halo-ce-universal.

You can now play the original Halo for free in your browser with 128-player multiplayer

Activision may have taken over the Halo series, but at least you can play the OG game in a browser now.

4
By  Patrick O'Rourke
